title: JavaScript basics
examples: How do I make a button do something when I click it?
What is the difference between using JavaScript and just HTML?
Where should I look to see if my code is working correctly?

explain.say: Today we are learning to make web pages interactive using JavaScript.
We use event listeners to wait for something to happen on the page.
When an event happens, we write a function to run in response.
The console is a special tool for seeing messages from your JavaScript code.
Let us see this in a real life example with a simple counter.
A common mistake is forgetting to select the element first.

items: This ensures the code finds the right target

faq.q: What is the difference between an event and an event listener?
faq.a: An event is the action itself, like a click. The event listener is the code that waits for and reacts to that action.
asks: How do I tell JavaScript to watch for something?

faq.q: Why do I need to use the console?
faq.a: The console lets you print messages to check if your code is running correctly. It is very useful for finding errors.
asks: Is the console like a notepad for code?
Where do I see errors when coding?

faq.q: Can I listen for multiple events on one element?
faq.a: Yes, you can attach multiple event listeners to the same element. For example, you can listen for both clicks and mouseovers.
asks: Can one button respond to two different things?
Is it possible to track multiple actions?

faq.q: Does JavaScript automatically know what I want to do?
faq.a: No, you must explicitly tell JavaScript what to do when an event happens. You have to write the function that handles the event.
asks: Do I need to write the response code?
What do I write after I detect the event?

faq.q: What if the element I want to listen to doesn't exist yet?
faq.a: If the element is not loaded when your script runs, the listener will fail. You might need to wait until the page is fully ready.
asks: When should I write the event listener code?
What if the HTML loads slowly?

facts: JavaScript uses event listeners to detect user actions like clicks.
The console is a browser tool used for debugging and viewing output.
An event handler is the function that executes when an event occurs.
You must select the HTML element before attaching an event listener to it.

quiz.say: If you want JavaScript to run code only when a user presses the Enter key, which event should you listen for?
quiz.why: The Keydown event fires immediately when a key is pressed down, which is what you need to detect the action.

wrong.0: Load detects when the entire page finishes loading, not a key press.
wrong.2: Click is for mouse buttons, not keyboard keys.
wrong.3: Mouseover only detects when the mouse moves over an area.

quiz.say: To check if a variable holds the value of pi, which tool is best for immediate feedback?
quiz.why: The console allows you to print variable values and test small pieces of code instantly.

wrong.1: HTML tags are for structure, not for running code checks.
wrong.2: CSS properties only control how things look on the screen.
wrong.3: An event listener waits for an action; it does not check values directly.

quiz.say: If you write 'document.getElementById("myButton").addEventListener("click", function(){...});', what is the purpose of the first part?

options.show: To find the specific HTML element on the page.
options.say: To find the specific HTML element on the page.

quiz.why: This code first locates the element using its ID before it can attach any behavior to it.

wrong.1: Adding an event listener makes the function wait for an event, it does not run it right away.
wrong.2: Changing text requires a different method, like innerHTML, not just selecting it.
wrong.3: The event type, like 'click', is passed as a separate argument, not part of the selection.
